title: The Seed Too Small to See
hook: a father has his son break a banyan seed until nothing is left to see; Vaisheshika asks where the breaking stops
tomorrow: a sage kicks Vishnu in the chest. what does Vishnu do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gleaner's handful outweighed a king's sacrifice, and Vaisheshika opened with dharma and with vishesha: each thing is itself. Now, the atoms.
screen: `DHARMA IS DONE IN PARTICULARS.` · `NOW, THE ATOMS.`

segments.voice: A young man named Shvetaketu has come home after twelve years of study, rather pleased with himself. His father, Uddalaka, isn't impressed yet. Bring me a fruit from that banyan tree, he says. Here it is. Break it. What do you see? Tiny seeds. Break one of those. What do you see now? Nothing at all, sir. And his father says: that fine thing you can't see, my son, out of that, this whole great banyan stands.
screen: `BREAK THE FRUIT.` → `BREAK THE SEED.` → `NOTHING YOU CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: That's the Chandogya Upanishad, and Uddalaka goes on: that finest essence is the self of the whole world. That is the real. That is the self. And that, Shvetaketu, is you: tat tvam asi. Centuries later, another Hindu school asked the same question, where does the breaking stop, and gave a different answer. Vaisheshika said the dividing stops at the paramanu, often translated atom: the smallest of the small. It has no parts, so it can't come apart, and the school calls it eternal, never made and never destroyed. You can't see one. So why believe it? Its thinkers argued: if you could divide forever, a mountain would have endless parts, and so would a mustard seed. Then what makes the mountain bigger? So the dividing must stop, at something partless. In the classic account, atoms pair up, the pairs gather, and you reach the smallest thing an eye can see: a speck of dust floating in a sunbeam. From there, up to clay and rivers and banyan trees. Atoms of earth, water, fire and air. So two answers, from one tradition. The Upanishad finds one unseen essence, and says it's you. Vaisheshika finds countless partless atoms, and many selves, which it names later this week. Hinduism keeps both on its shelf, and this path ranks neither. What they share is the teaching: what you see stands on what you can't, and the unseen doesn't break. A cup breaks; a body ages. For Vaisheshika, the breaking happens in the joints, not at the bottom of things.
screen: `TAT TVAM ASI: THAT, YOU ARE.` · `PARAMANU: THE SMALLEST OF THE SMALL.` · `A MOUNTAIN AND A MUSTARD SEED.` · `A SPECK IN A SUNBEAM.` · then, large: `THE BREAKING IS IN THE JOINTS.`

segments.voice: Hold a seed, a grain of rice, or just look at your own hand. Imagine breaking it in half, and again, down past what any eye can see. Then let one thing that has come apart lately come to mind, a plan, a routine, maybe something more, without fixing it, and notice that what it was made of, the care, the time, hasn't simply vanished. If you pray, rest in what you trust doesn't come apart. If you don't, rest in the breath.
Vaisheshika. The school of particulars and of the paramanu: the partless smallest thing, where all dividing has to stop.
Your line: paramanu, where all dividing stops. The unseen holds up the banyan. Back tomorrow, same hill.

screen: `DAY 1167 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES VISHNU DO WHEN HE'S KICKED?`
